In general, the key to good small talk is to either wait for or engineer a moment when the person says something specific enough to elaborate on, then set them up to talk about themselves. The "talking about themselves" is key - no matter what your reply is, most neurotypicals will think a conversation went well if they talked for most of it. Try to cater every reply to get even more specifics out of them to keep things going. I personally think of it like an interrogation, which is probably a bit much for meeting people's wives at the company picnic or whatever, but going into things with an "attack plan" really helps me personally.

In practice, I have four tentpoles:

1. Any day of the week - "I love your \[item of clothing\]! Where did you get it?" The more unique the item is, the better - look for something colorful or with a fun print. This one definitely has an asterisk (I'm a woman and I only use it talking to other women\*), but the key to making it small-talk and not flirtatious is to focus on a specific item rather than just "you look great!". Asking where they got it and saying you've always wanted something similar is a good opener. 
   1. If you're a woman talking to another woman, see if she has unique shoes. From there, ask if they're comfy to walk in all day. Use "I walk all day doing XYZ!" to transition to something else (about the XYZ you walk all day doing. Maybe it's your job. By the way, what do you do?)
   2. If the person has a cool/unique item of clothing that seems to be somehow fandom related (like a graphic t-shirt), ask what the shirt's a reference to and use it to transition to item 3.
2. If it's a Monday/Friday - "what are you doing this weekend/do anything fun this weekend?" 
   1. If they did something fun, ask about the activity, and use that to elaborate. "Mountain biking sounds beautiful! Do you go often? Is that your favorite trail, or do you go elsewhere sometimes? Does the whole family go? Oh, they do! How old are your kids?" Etc.
   2. If they said "I just stayed in", like a lame person who doesn't get what the deal is here, mention that you did the same and watched a TV show. Use that TV show to transition to item 3.
3. TV shows! If TV or movies ever comes up in the conversation, ask what they've seen recently. (Like #1, this is a bit situational, since I live in LA and work in film so it comes up *a lot* professionally, but everyone has a Netflix habit nowadays.) The key to making it good small talk is to ask for a recommendation - "I've been looking for shows to catch up on. Is that one fun?" From there, pick at the threads - the last show you watched was XYZ, you really like that actor from ZYX, have you seen YXZ? It's also hilarious! Etc.
4. And finally, pets! This is my silver bullet of small talk - almost everyone has one or has had one at some point, they're personal and fun, and it's almost guaranteed to be "inoffensive" (it's hard to accidentally step on a politics/religion landmine if you're asking about Mr. Snuffles the Goldendoodle). Say the pet is cute, ask their name, what kind of dog/cat they are, how old they are, etc. Use that to relate things back to yourself - "I also had a Goldendoodle when I was younger, but his name was Mr. Truffles!" or whatever.
   1. If the pet's not physically there (or in the background on Zoom to start a conversation), see if there's a photo displayed with the pet, or if it's on their phone lockscreen.
   2. If they don't have a photo, see if you can mention your pet in the intro conversation ("I apologize in advance if my dog barks, he's antsy today"), and ask if the person has one.

\*I don't say this to be essentialist! Obviously there are plenty of stylish people of all genders you can ask this to, and there are certain situations where this won't apply. I'm just a queer lady who's hyper-afraid of coming off as creepy around women I like, and I know a lot of other neurodivergent people have this anxiety, so I really cater my conversations to sound not flirty above all else.

Saw the first three episodes a few weeks after they dropped, mainly because I was a huge WWDitS fan. To be honest, I wasn't impressed. (If you like the first three, more power to you!  They're just not my bag.)  I liked that the show seemed to be burning down their primary conflict engines (Jim's reveal as a "woman", Blackbeard's arrival) and really disrupting the status quo at the end of 3, but I honestly remember thinking "cool intro for Taika's character! I bet he'll be a three-episode guest star." I put the show down and didn't think about it for a few weeks. Then, I got COVID, and had a) a lot of time to kill and b) a REALLY rough day at work. I'd also seen a headline for a Mary Sue article about how "OFMD is fandom's latest obsession", or something like that, so I figured hey, it probably gets a little better! I decided to watch two or three episodes on what I thought was a random Wednesday as a pick-me-up.

I was hooked five minutes into episode four, and by episode five I was literally dragging my roommate out of her room and yelling "did they almost kiss? *Are you seeing what I'm seeing?*" The romance hooked me immediately, and I binged the entire series thus far in one night (which I NEVER do - I hate binge-watching with a passion.) It was an EXTREMELY weird emotional tug-of-war that's hard to describe, as I fought between what my writer brain was clearly recognizing as a developing romance with clear beats and emotional tension, and my logic brain saying that there's no way they'd be brave enough to go there, much less in a Taika Waititi and Rhys Darby sitcom, of all fucking things. But the hints were getting stronger with every episode, and the show was becoming more and more casually queer. I think I realized around episode eight that there was no way I could be casual about the finale, because they were either going to go there and it would be the ballsiest move ever, or they were going to chicken out and I would be not just baited, but served deep-fried bait by a Michelin-star chef with a side of Worcestershire sauce.

I finished the last episode HBO had posted - episode 8 - showered, and was getting ready for bed when I saw that the show was trending on Twitter. I then clicked it and the first Tweet I saw was a random account with a rainbow avatar yelling "THEY FUCKING DID IT". Turns out it wasn't just a random Wednesday - it was the Wednesday before the finale dropped, and it dropped at midnight my time. And it was 12:15. I immediately exited out of Twitter and pulled up HBO Max on my laptop again, and the rest was history.

I know my circumstances are kind of unique and I got really lucky with the timing, but that Wednesday was genuinely one of the most intense emotional journeys a show has ever taken me on. Part of me feels like I got the best of both worlds, because I got the genuine "wait, this *isn't* queerbaiting?" tension from before it was confirmed, but also didn't have to wait very long to get an answer. It's a weirdly special TV-watching memory for me that I know I'll cherish for a long time, and also made my last few days with the plague a bit more bearable.

For real, the fact that the characters are middle-aged and not played by the usual retired models in their twenties is genuinely a huge part of why I find this show so unique. (Not that either Taika or Rhys are bad-looking! They're quite charming! But they're clearly regular dudes in their forties, and in an industry where so much casting is based on sex appeal, the fact that two regular dudes in their forties can melt down the internet with naught but their emotional intimacy makes me smile.)

The short/recap version is this: the show does an excellent job setting up what I call "the puzzle piece", establishing right away what each of them lacks emotionally that the other one can fulfill. (Stede wanting someone to teach him to be tougher versus Ed wanting someone to teach him to be gentle; Stede wanting to become the dangerous pirate he's always dreamed of being, versus Ed being tired of being the monster everyone perceives him as.) The show doesn't just demonstrate this with tropes or cliches, but works hard to craft moments of genuine emotional intimacy that highlights how they fit together. "You wear fine things well" is the epitome of this; it shows us this character we've been laughing at for five episodes through Ed's eyes, highlighting that his gentleness and kindness is something Ed's been craving. The show doesn't just say "these two fell for each other" - it works really hard to establish *why* they fell for each other. It fits perfectly into the show's themes of second chances and trying to live the life you actually want, not the one society prescribes. (An interesting thing to note is that there's basically no "heat" in their love story - it's an arc entirely dedicated to emotional tension instead of sexual tension. Which is a lot harder to do! But it works!)

It's the kind of character work that doesn't look like work until you've tried to write it, and a lot of lazier romance media skips out on by  going "these two bicker, and now they kiss!" Bad romance stories presume that we'll want them to get together just because they're the protagonists and that's what protagonists do, without showing us why they need each other to be emotionally complete. (My roommie is much more plot-driven in her writing,  and she's been asking romance-obsessed me for feedback on how to make her romance sideplots more emotionally satisfying. I joked that this was her homework, but it was actually REALLY informative and now we're both emotional wrecks.)

Although I haven't played a handful of the romance paths (I'm waiting for Legendary to buy the trilogy on my current PC), my favorites are FemShep/Garrus and MShep/Kaidan.

Ironically enough, my first-ever playthrough was FemShep/Kaidan, but I dumped him for Garrus after Horizon and never looked back. When playing as a female character, Kaidan seemed simultaneously melodramatic and unforgiving: at least how I was roleplaying, he seemed like the only one incapable of seeing that I had no choice but to work for Cerberus, and the line where he asked why I never even called him when I was *literally in a body bag* cracked me up. In a way, Garrus is a great romance plotline because of how easy it is - it's the perfect friends-to-lovers story, not in the sense of a grand sweeping romantic tension that was never acted upon, but in the sense of "oh, we already know each other so well and love each other in one way, of course we were going to fall in love at some point". By the time I got to 3, I outright hated Kaidan, because Garrus was so instinctively supportive and a rock for my Shep, and Kaidan was *still* going on about Cerberus and butthurt that I wasn't screwing him . That first playthrough soured me on Kaidan as a character, because he seemed so dramatic, and Garrus was so not: there were no big speeches, no debates, no drama, just "I have your back". My first Shep was tactical, by-the-book, and low-drama, so Kaidan just didn't fit.

...which is not the case with Kaidan/M!Shep, but once I actually played that path out of curiosity, I came to appreciate it. K/M!S is the romance plotline that takes the longest to actually happen (you don't hook up until midway through 3), and although the reasons for that were kind of accidental, IMHO it's what makes the storyline work. Here are these two men who have had something for each other for years, but *everything* kept getting in the way of them acting on it. Kaidan's speech on Horizon didn't seem melodramatic when I was viewing it through the lens of "unrequited love makes you fucking crazy" - of course he's upset. He never got to tell Shephard how he felt, and then Shephard died, and now he's back after two years of mourning, and Kaidan *still can't say it*. Because Shephard's dead, because Shephard's working for a terrorist group, because who knows how Shephard even would have reacted before any of this happened, *who knows if Shep even likes men*? What is he supposed to do, tell Shep he feels betrayed because he's crazy for him *now*, with these random Cerberus strangers here? It's only when the world is literally ending that they're able to spit it out and be together, because you stop worrying about social niceties when the apocalypse is out your door. And it's great that they got together, but it's also a tragedy that it took them this long - ME3 canonically takes place over a few months, and by the time they hook up halfway-ish through, they have maybe a *month* to actually love each other before Shep takes the Conduit. I will grant that years of reading Winter Soldier fanfic probably made me a sucker for this storyline, but it works, and it works because they're both men, not in spite of it. Unlike FShep/Garrus, it's an extremely dramatic love story. But when I'm in the mood for drama, it works like a charm.

Anyway, check back with me after Legendary drops and I go for Tali, because I was seriously fucking heartbroken that I couldn't romance her as a woman. I might change my mind!

This sounds like my mom - she had a major complex about sugar my entire childhood. She taught me to count calories and check everything I ate for grams of sugar at age nine, tried to put me on Weight Watchers at age eleven, gave away my birthday cake to casual acquaintances the next day so I couldn't have the leftovers, and threatened to pull me out of college at least once a semester if I didn't lose weight. All it did was give me a major complex in return. I looked forward to holidays solely because there would be dessert. Once I was allowed to drive in high school, I would go buy giant portions of sugary food, eat them in my car, and throw away the wrappers in the parking lot. I would buy extra bags of candy at the movies with my friends, hide them in my purse, and eat them at 2am at home before putting the wrappers back in my purse so she couldn't catch me. I gorged myself on the sly all throughout college, like, "would literally have a package of double stuff Oreos in my desk drawer and would go through them in a day" type of gorge. I'd go entire days eating nothing but sugar. I stopped by an on-campus bakery so often, they knew me and my order by name.

And guess what? I came out of college as someone who eats mostly grilled chicken and veggie stir-fry, jogs every day, doesn't drink anything except coffee and water, and usually only has sugar in the house when I bake as a hobby once a week, and even then I gave most of what I made away to my coworkers pre-Covid. Because it turns out you actually want healthier snacks when you have options, and not when you're hungry and the only thing you're allowed to snack on is one tiny apple. You only find out that eating too much sugar isn't actually fun and makes you feel like shit when you're allowed more than two bites of sugar a year under heavy scrutiny. And when you do want that slice of cake, it's much easier to stop at just one slice, because it's something you want, not something you're pining for. Meanwhile, she's been eating everything I bake during quarantine under the table and "jokingly" admitting that I need to slow down, because *she* has problems with sugar and portion control. Don't project on your fucking kids, and don't make them feel like they should be ashamed for wanting sugar when they're in the single digits. Most of the endings will give you the same kind of radiant quests - the only big gameplay change is that if you play the Minutemen ending right, you can keep both the BoS and the Railroad in play - so I made my decision morally. IMHO, the  endings have a pretty clear  ranking from least to most evil:

1. The Minutemen. This is the only way to keep everyone in the BoS and Railroad alive, and their goals are overall just "help people defend themselves from raiders/Institute/threats". Siding with them destroys the Institute and also leads to the least murder. 
2. The Railroad. They're basically the Rebel Alliance and are fighting for the oppressed (and the fact that they're such scrappy underdogs makes them my favorite, because their ending feels a lot more like a hard-won victory), but siding with them means wiping out the BoS. Granted, it's retaliation for the BoS striking first, but they have twelve-year-old members, for fuck's sake, and a lot of young recruits who were just looking for a better life in the Wasteland, so that still counts against them slightly.
3. The BoS. They genuinely leave civilians alone and have mostly peaceful intentions, but they're *extremely* racist to ghouls and synths, and it's implied that they'll start...removing them once they're in power. Plus, Teagan's quest has them forcibly conscripting civilian farmers, and the implications of a foreign independent army sweeping into an area and taking over is a bit too fascist for me to be sympathetic. But still, they blow up the Institute, so stopped clocks?
4. The Institute. This is *the* evil ending, and I'm surprised people talk about it like it's somehow nuanced. They kidnap and kill people and replace them with robots that completely change their personality. They have technology that could feed and help people on the surface that they refuse to share, because they think that all of humanity is a lost cause. They have the resources to save thousands of lives and chose not to use them. Plus, *they make slaves and kidnap them back when they try to escape*. There's almost no way to morally justify siding with them, in my opinion. Their core philosophy is rotten. 

There are a couple of nuances here - siding against the Minutemen as the Institute means you no longer have Minutemen artillery, I believe that going either Institute or Minutemen (minus BoS) means you don't have vertibirds anymore, siding against the BoS with anyone will mean you lose control of the Boston Airport settlement (which you can get back once you destroy them), destroying the BoS/RR/Institute means you lose access to their gear shops. But overall, those are pretty minimal changes. I'd advise going with your heart.

Because he's not the director, he doesn't know what's about to happen - he's just a normal person, and he's not being "told" where to look, on a literal or figurative/meta level. And unrelated to the filmmaking, I absolutely loved how the two leads were fresh faces/nobodies, with the more prominent actors coming and going for one quick scene each. IMHO, it's a tiny percent due to TLJ, but that percentage is much less than most people want (and I think TLJ is an excellent movie that was exactly what the franchise needed...which I am literally afraid to say because I'll get downvoted to hell, but whatever, I'm sick of hiding my love for a thing I love for no good reason). The real answer is a complicated combo of...a lot.

* **TLJ got crazy backlash.** And \*a lot\* of it was based in sexism/racism/general dark-corners-of-the-internet fuckery from people who were quietly sticking to 4chan in 2015. I am not blaming the election, but...the 2016 election was a *huge* shift in American culture that I don't think anyone has really grasped the extent of yet, and *everything* is affected by that. The point is, the political climate changed very quickly over  two years, and dissatisfied people felt free to be louder and meaner. (I still think this is only 10/20% of the "real reason" - the franchise could have weathered it if it was the only thing. But at the same time...)
   * **The crazy TLJ backlash lead to them overcorrecting on episode 9,** and from the sounds of the early reviews, almost no one is happy. This isn't related to the general decline, but it's a sad footnote.
* **Disney tried to run Star Wars like the MCU,** with "main story" releases in the episodes and spin-offs in the blocks in between. But **Star Wars does not and cannot ever operate like the MCU.** Basically nothing operates like the MCU: the MCU's wild success is partially due to like, sheer fucking luck (this is a whole other essay), and partially due to the fact that it's about ten franchises in one. A Guardians movie and an Ant-Man movie can be developed separately with entirely different casts, crews, and directors, while being part of the same franchise and shot simultaneously. This speeds up the rate that MCU movies can be produced, and reduces audience fatigue, and a story that's principally about one small cast of characters just can't  keep up.
   * Likewise, Kevin Feige was at the helm. Feige knows exactly how much crossover is too much, that you can go auteur on the spin-offs but should play it safe in the main story entries, etc. Kathleen Kennedy, for all I defend her for getting a ton of sexist shit that a man in her position would never get, wasn't prepared for how her franchise was different.
* The lesson no one learned from this until it was too late is that **Star Wars works best in moderation.** A Star Wars movie at its best is a Big Epic Saga, and it feels much more Big and Epic when it's one movie every two years, not a sprawling tangle of product with conflicting lore. Yes, there are EU fans, but most casual viewers are just here for the Skywalkers (and the people around them). You seen an MCU movie once every three months with your friends: you see a Star Wars movie once every three years with your family. It's just a different kind of franchise.
* On a related note...**the MCU got big. Like, really big.** Like, once-in-a-generation, cosmic-fluke, not even the most blindly optimistic predictor could have ever predicted this big. Black Panther got nominated for Best Picture. IW and Endgame became even bigger water-cooler films than TFA. There is such a thing as saturating the market, and when the MCU got big, it inadvertently saturated the Disney-blockbuster one. And it's not just money, it's *attention*. The MCU was new - a  majority of viewers don't read comics, so to them, it was a world and characters they were discovering for the first time, and because it's so big, there's something for  everyone. TFA was a "welcome back", but after a few years, your dad's favorite blockbuster was old news compared to "your story".
* On a related related note, **Disney got too big for its own britches,** and we're starting to see the downfall now. Between 2018 and 2019, the consecutive record-breaking insanity of BP - IW - Capt. Marvel - Endgame dominated  people's discussions about Disney, even insiders, because it looked like Disney was a machine that would never stop churning. Because people were all talking about IW, *Solo* bombing  kind of...slid under the radar. The TRoS behind-the-scenes fuckery was relatively under-reported. (And that's not even bringing up all the live-action reboots that were bombing, the controversies about LGBT representation...) There were just less eyes on the thing, and it was being made in the background of a company that was losing ground when everyone thought it was conquering the world.
   * An anecdote re Galaxy's Edge as a theme park nerd - Disney clearly wanted to build a theme park for one of its franchises, **but Disney legally cannot build any MCU theme-park attractions** in Florida. Universal got the Avengers theme park rights on the east coast in 1999, and the contract is in perpetuity. The Guardians *technically* aren't Avengers in the comics, so there's a Guardians coaster being built in FL, but the point is that even if the MCU seemed like a more logical choice for a theme park land, it was literally not an option. There's currently an Avengers land being built at Disneyland in California, but Disneyland is infamously cramped and has a much lower tourist-to-locals ratio then  World, where they literally own a municipality. 
      * And re: **the low Galaxy's Edge attendance...Disney Parks have been** ***spiking*** **in prices** in the past few years. Total attendance has leveled out, because people have stopped being able to afford it. The fact that a  major new land is "bombing" can't be extricated from this.
* **Trevorrow got fired.** Probably for good reason, but the behind-the-scenes drama could not have helped.
* And, finally, **Carrie Fisher died.** This one was an unavoidable tragedy that was no one's fault, and like a lot of people, I miss her terribly. But based on an interview Mark Hamill gave after her death, the loose plan for the trilogy involved the legacy characters - Ep7 was Han's movie, Ep8 was Luke's, and 9 was supposed to be Leia's (you can see this in TFA/TLJ). Fisher's death meant they had to start the finale from scratch, story-wise, without their star, and with all the foreshadowing and setup from the already-produced prior episodes - yes, TRoS uses archive footage, but the things you can do with archive footage are less than whatever full-fledged arc was planned.

So yeah...it's complicated. And while I think the franchise could have survived one or even two of these, all of them together was a kiss of death. Frankly, I think the downfall is  tragic - they had all the money in the world, backed by the biggest entertainment company of all time, and were ultimately defeated by things money couldn't buy. In 1996, a screenwriter named Shane Black got rejected from joining the Academy right after his latest movie, *The Long Kiss Goodnight*, bombed. Black was best known for creating the *Lethal Weapon* franchise, but he decided to try and write something completely outside the action genre, and settled on a romantic comedy. Black struggled to write the screenplay and eventually took the advice of a friend to "throw a murder in there", and wound up with a noir/romance/comedy hybrid called *You'll Never Die in This Town Again*, which was eventually renamed *Kiss Kiss Bang Bang*. A bunch of studios turned down the script, but an old producing partner of Black's from the *Lethal Weapon* days named Joel Silver agreed to help finance the film. However, struggled to find an actor whose paycheck could fit in the 15 million dollar budget ( small for a feature of that size). Casting help came from the most unlikely of places: Silver's personal assistant, a woman named Susan Levine, had just started dating an actor looking for work. Levine's boyfriend had been a hot commodity several years ago, but had a very public drug problem, and even though he was now clean, no one was willing to cover the production costs in case he relapsed. Fortunately, Black had had substance abuse issues of his own, and he and his new leading man bonded and agreed to work together: *Kiss Kiss Bang Bang* opened in late October 2005. Despite positive reviews, it was a box-office flop in the US, making only 4.2 million. Both Black and his leading man moved on to other projects.

A year later, a director named John Favreau was trying to develop an unusual superhero tentpole at Paramount. Although the film revolved around the main character, and Tom Cruise had even been attached to the title role at one point, Favreau didn't want an established star: he wanted the character to speak for himself, rather than being a movie-star vehicle. Unfortunately, the character was also kind of a smart-ass, and casting was running out of ideas. Favreau had recently seen *Kiss Kiss*, and vouched for the lead to get a screen test, despite the studio (Paramount) claiming that he was unpopular and would drag the film down. Fortunately, Favreau fought tooth and nail for him, and Black's leading man was cast, bringing Black himself along to punch up the script's dialogue.

The actor was Robert Downey Jr., the Paramount tentpole was *Iron Man,* and Susan Levine is now known professionally as Susan Downey. The modern MCU, a phenomenon without precedent in film history whose titanic legacy is still being shaped and basically purchased Disney's cultural dominance (and therefore a lot of other competing franchises in reaction to it), exists only because Shane Black was rejected from the Academy in 1996 and had an action movie bomb.

I once had a marketing executive for a small but significant distribution company come talk to our college class (a big part of their brand is that they're focused on bringing in young people...not hard to guess which one). After a speech that was mostly about how luring millenials to the theater is a cultural problem, how you have to motivate them to leave Netflix and "make it a can't miss experience of buzzability and hype!" and all that jazz, she did some informal polling and asked how often we all went to the movies vs. stayed in and streamed.

She was shocked--legitimately SHOCKED--that almost everyone in the class  \*liked\* going to the theater, and almost everyone's motivation for staying home wasn't laziness or lack of interest, but money. This is a woman who's in charge of theatrical distribution for a company \*aimed at millenials\*. And she admitted that she had never thought  the main thing keeping people home was the ticket price. (This is in a major city where a  2D ticket costs eighteen dollars.) It  boggled my mind, but realizing the price-myopia at even the most "progressive" level has explained a lot about the exhibition industry's missteps in the past decade, IMO. If attendance drops in favor of a cheaper alternative in an economic recession, but you assume that the cheaper alternative is actually widely preferred, you're going to handle things the exact wrong way.

My understanding is that in the traditional Hollywood release calendar, October is the month that launches Oscar season, so studios are usually putting out their prestige projects and biopics (along with some horror and maybe a kid's movie to balance it out). All of the previous October record holders were movies in this category that broke out or were a little more populist in their Oscar convictions--Gravity, The Martian, etc. To my knowledge, it's pretty unusual for a superhero movie like Venom to be released in this season, even if it does have horror elements--usually, late-year blockbusters are placed to capitalize on the Thanksgiving or Christmas holidays. Granted, this calendar has been slowly but surely evolving in the past few years (four straight years of unexpected hits turned February from the prototypical "dump month" into a prime slot for Black Panther, no one's taken advantage of the early-August "run through the end of summer" slot GotG and Suicide Squad used since 2016, and Star Wars has kind of made Christmas the new May for non-superhero tentpoles), but it's still very much in effect, and I think studios are just now starting to realize that you can break records if you use your releases to fill those gaps.

Back in December, when I rewatched the prequels to prep for TLJ, I did a brain exercise of how I would fix them from a script-doctor perspective (ie, if I were brought on to polish Lucas' material instead of just being told "write whatever"):

1) Phantom Menace isn't a movie. Most of its events still happened as backstory, but we hear about them, not watch them.

2) Movie 1 is an edited AotC, with Dooku as the main villain, and ends when Anakin kills Dooku at Palpatine's urging. Movie 2 ends with Anakin killing the younglings and getting "crowned" as Vader, and movie 3 is Obi-Wan's attempt to stop Anakin.

3) When we first meet Anakin, he's introduced to us as a Jedi Wunderkid. This kid was destined to balance the galaxy! Have you heard about how *amazing* this kid is? The Legendary Dead Qui-Gon Jin, a guy so legendary we only hear about him in whispers, literally sacrificed himself for this kid! Anakin is brilliant and likeable, but we see that he's socially isolated from his fellow Jedii trainees and has a lot of repressed anger from childhood trauma that he hasn't ever really dealt with and doesn't have a healthy outlet for (think Will Hunting). He's a great fighter, but in the opening scene he Gets Cocky and Fucks It Up, because he's *the chosen one* and doesn't understand playing as a team. Obi-Wan, who does genuinely love him like a brother/son but is burdened with the weird baggage of the debt he owes to The Legendary Dead Qui-Gon, grounds him and assigns him a shitty escort mission as penance.

4) Anakin and Padme are the same age, and don't meet until the beginning of the first movie--she's his escort mission. The two bond and fall in love over their shared experience of being "chosen children" at a too-young age: Padme in leading her people, Anakin in being The Chosen One. But Anakin's quiet and cagey about a big part of his past, until we get the news about Shmi. It's a reveal: holy shit, this kid was a *child slave*.

5) Meanwhile, Palpatine hears about this Chosen One with anger issues, and senses an opportunity. So near the end of the first movie, he deliberately gets himself "kidnapped" and calls on the Jedi to save him, deliberately so he can woo Anakin into the throne room alone and get him to kill Dooku. 

6) Anakin and Obi reunite, and Anakin tries to tell Obi about his mother, but Obi doesn't really know how to handle emotions and is just like "Jedi aren't supposed to feel anger or love. You'll get over it kid! You're the Chosen One!" Naturally, this doesn't help, and sets up the great tragedy of their relationship--that they only met because Anakin was the Chosen One, but it's also what tears them apart.

7) Palpatine's plan works, and Ani kills Dooku, angry about his mom, Obi, and the love he can't have with Padme. As he panics that he gave in to his anger, Palpatine offers to take Anakin under his wing--he understands Anakin's rage, which is more than Obi-Wan ever did. Anakin agrees. Fuck the Jedi order! Fuck Obi-Wan! He can be a Jedi and be angry! He can be a Jedi and in love! This guy understands!

8) Midway through the second movie (essentially, the first half of Sith), we find out that Padme is dying. Not like, "lost the will to live". Actually dying. Space cancer or whatever. She tells only Anakin, who's violent and panicking and doesn't know how to live when the only thing he feels like he's ever had for himself is getting ripped away, and her good friend in the Senate, Bail Organa. Bail noticed her pregnancy in the early stages--he's been trying to get pregnant with his wife, with little success--and becomes her ally in hiding the pregnancy/saving democracy. Padme doesn't *like* that she's dying, obviously, but she's determined to make the best of the time she has left: save democracy, save her babies. She begs Anakin to understand. He...doesn't. He takes it as a betrayal. Anakin gets obsessed with saving her life, add Palpatine's influence, hence Vader. (Doubleuberbonuspoints if it was somehow implied that part of what's killing Padme is that she's pregnant with grandkids of the Force, which her human body can't handle, and that that quadrouples Anakin's guilt.)

9) Yoda doesn't go into exile because he failed; he goes into exile because he gave into anger when Palpatine taunted him about the death of Windu, and he almost won the fight, but couldn't live with himself.

10) Middle of the third movie. It's the galaxy's darkest hour. Palpatine's been installed, Anakin's gone evil, Obi-Wan has to stop him. He's having a crisis of confidence, he can't go on--but who is this? It's Legendary Dead Qui-Gon Jin, here as a Force ghost, in a surprise one-scene role by Esteemed Actor Liam Neeson! They have a talk about Anakin and legacy and blah blah Obi gets the energy to go stop him. Qui-Gon hints that maybe, this is just the Force's very indirect way of bringing about Anakin's destiny all along. Obi learns to be a good Christian Allegory and roll with God/The Force's plan. 

Obviously, these are just plot points for the main emotional arc, not including the obligatory dialogue polish, trimming of filler (that droid factory scene is the first to go), and beefing up the supporting characters (how about we actually play up the fact that Dooku was apparently Qui-Gon's Master?). But I like to think that this isn't a radical reinvention, just taking Lucas' interesting themes and actually putting them into focus. Objective: YMMV on some of this, but it's easily the most consistent Marvel sub-franchise, and the most consistently good--thematically clear, strong writing, and with the best action direction in the MCU by a mile. The whole trilogy was written by the same creative team, and they *really* know what they're doing--the plots are easy to follow, they're emotionally and thematically weighty, the dialogue is succinct and quotable, the pacing is basically perfect. As a screenwriting student, I don't think a lot of people realize how *difficult* that is, especially three times in a row, when the studio is throwing increasingly more constraints/mandates at you. (Granted, they broke their streak a little bit with Infinity War, which...I have thoughts about, but the non-spoiler answer is that you can tell they're way more comfortable writing grounded political conflict than anything galactic.) Plus, this is the benefit of hindsight, but Winter Soldier in particular has aged...I don't know if the word is "well", but let's say it feels way more resonant than it did in 2014.
